div.p: This page is a single, central point explaining the real, technical things hams.com does to protect you -- your credentials, your transmitter, and your ability to verify any of this for yourself rather than just taking our word for it. Each section below is a short, honest summary; follow the link for the full detail. Nothing on this page describes a protection that isn't actually true of the running system today -- where something is designed but not yet shipped, that's said plainly, not rounded up.
div.h3: Your LoTW certificate never touches our application
div.p: hams.com's application code never receives your ARRL Logbook of the World certificate or its private key, in any form, at any point -- verification happens entirely at the TLS layer, before your request ever reaches our application.

p.a: Read the full LoTW Trust and Certificate Custody page →

div.h3: We can never remotely control your transmitter
div.p: The local relay software that connects your radio to hams.com enforces a frequency safety interlock directly against your radio's own live state, immediately before every key-on. This is local configuration on your own machine, changeable only by physical access to it -- designed to keep holding even if hams.com's own central servers were ever fully compromised.

p.a: Read the full Transmitter Safety Commitments page →

div.h3: Disclosed source: you can read what the relay software actually does
div.p: The local relay daemon that talks to your radio stays proprietary software -- publishing its source isn't a license change -- but its real source is published at /relay/source for anyone to inspect directly, rather than asking you to trust a description of code you can't see. This is the same software responsible for the frequency-safety interlock above and your LoTW credential handling.

The relay daemon verifies every self-update against a cryptographic signature before installing it, so a compromise of the release infrastructure alone can't push malicious code to already-running daemons. Separately, we've verified directly -- not just claimed -- that building the daemon from a given commit and a pinned toolchain produces a byte-for-byte identical binary every time, meaning an outside reviewer can build the published source themselves and check that the result matches what we ship.

Honestly disclosed gap: the real signing keypair that will link a specific published-source commit to a specific signed release binary hasn't been generated yet -- the published-source page shows "not yet signed" rather than a real signature today. This page will be updated the day that changes, not before.
div.h3: A revoked daemon version warns you loudly -- it doesn't get bricked
div.p: If a released daemon version is ever found to have a real problem, hams.com can mark that specific version as revoked. The daemon tries to update itself immediately -- but if that update fails, it does not silently stop working. By design it keeps running and warns as loudly as it can, and only blocks new transmissions if that specific revocation was separately marked critical by a human curator, not as a blanket policy. Your radio stays usable unless there's a specifically-flagged safety reason for it not to be.

None of these protections depend on trusting hams.com's servers to stay honest or uncompromised forever: the frequency interlock lives on your own machine, the source is published for you to read, the builds are reproducible so you can confirm what you're actually running, and updates are cryptographically verified before they ever install. Where a gap is still open, it's named here specifically so you know exactly what to check yourself in the meantime, not glossed over.
